task: Audit a firm's exposure in each foreign market and rank the markets by how far they sit from home.
condition: Given a firm's sales, cost and supplier figures for at least four countries and a set of public country data.
standard: Every share, score and loss figure is calculated correctly, and the ranking is backed by written reasons.
who: Senior managers and directors who must decide where a firm should grow, hold or pull back abroad.

modules.title: Mapping revenue and cost exposure by country
modules.bloom: Remember and apply: list and calculate
modules.intro: Exposure means how much of the firm depends on each country. We start by turning raw figures into shares.
points: Exposure = share of sales, costs, assets and staff
Add the shares up to check they reach 100%
A concentration score shows how spread out the firm is
modules.example: A firm sells 200m a year: home 120m, country B 40m, country C 24m, country D 16m. Shares are 60%, 20%, 12% and 8%. Concentration score = 0.60 squared + 0.20 squared + 0.12 squared + 0.08 squared = 0.36 + 0.04 + 0.0144 + 0.0064 = 0.4208. A score of 1.0 means one country only. A score of 0.25 means four equal countries. At 0.42 the firm leans heavily on home.
modules.activity: Using a table of sales, costs and staff for five countries, calculate the share of each and the concentration score for sales and for costs.
modules.standard: All shares add to 100% within 0.5 points and both scores are correct to two decimals.

modules.title: Measuring distance between two markets
modules.bloom: Understand and apply: explain and score
modules.intro: Distance is more than kilometres. It has cultural, rule-based, physical and economic parts.
points: Four distance types: cultural, administrative, geographic, economic
Score each type 1 (close) to 5 (far)
Weight scores by the firm's product
modules.example: A food maker compares home with a target market. Scores: cultural 4, administrative 2, geographic 3, economic 5. Fresh food depends on shipping, so weights are cultural 20%, administrative 20%, geographic 40%, economic 20%. Weighted score = 0.2x4 + 0.2x2 + 0.4x3 + 0.2x5 = 0.8 + 0.4 + 1.2 + 1.0 = 3.4 out of 5. A plain sum of 14 would hide that shipping matters most.
modules.activity: Score two target markets on all four distance types for a product of your choice, choose weights, and state which market is nearer.
modules.standard: Eight scores each have a one-line reason, weights add to 100%, and the weighted totals are correct.

modules.title: Currency exposure and hedge ratios
modules.intro: Money earned in one currency and spent in another can move profit without any change in the business. We measure the gap and decide how much to cover.
points: Net exposure = receipts minus payments in that currency
A move of x% changes profit by x% of net exposure
A hedge ratio is the share of exposure covered
modules.example: A plant has euro costs of 30m and euro sales of 10m. Net short position = 30m - 10m = 20m euro. If the euro rises 10%, cost rises 2m. The board sets a 60% hedge: 0.6 x 20m = 12m covered. Open position = 8m, so the same 10% move now costs 0.8m instead of 2m.
modules.activity: Given receipts and payments in three currencies, work out net exposure in each and the open loss from a 10% move at a 50% hedge.
modules.standard: Net positions and open losses are correct for all three currencies.

modules.title: Political and legal risk scoring
modules.intro: Some risks come from rules and governments, not from the market. We turn them into scores that can be compared.
points: List risks: tax change, expropriation, sanctions, contract enforcement
Give each a chance and an impact
Risk score = chance x impact
modules.example: For country C: tax rise, chance 40%, impact 3m a year, so 1.2m. Contract dispute, chance 25%, impact 8m, so 2.0m. Sanctions, chance 5%, impact 40m, so 2.0m. Total expected loss = 1.2 + 2.0 + 2.0 = 5.2m. The rare sanction risk is as large as the common dispute risk, so it needs its own plan.
modules.activity: Build a risk table of five risks for one country with chances and impacts and rank them by expected loss.
modules.standard: Five risks, correct products, a correct total and a ranked list with one sentence on the top item.

modules.title: Supply-chain concentration
modules.intro: A firm can look spread out on sales but depend on one supplier country. We test how much a failure would cost.
points: List suppliers by share of inputs
Estimate weeks of outage
Lost output = share x outage weeks / 52 x annual output
modules.example: Annual output is 130m. Supplier shares: country X 55%, Y 25%, Z 20%. If X fails for 6 weeks and nothing can replace it: 130m x 0.55 x 6/52 = 8.25m of lost output. If a backup supplier can cover half of X, loss = 4.13m. Paying 1.0m a year to keep the backup is worth it if such a failure is expected more often than once in four years.
modules.activity: For a supplier table you are given, calculate the loss from the loss of each country for 4 weeks and name the highest.
modules.standard: All three loss figures correct and the largest correctly identified.

modules.title: Comparing market-entry options
modules.intro: Selling by export, by licence or through a local company has different cost, control and risk. We compare them on the same numbers.
points: Compare setup cost, yearly profit and risk
Use a simple payback in years
Match the option to the distance scores
modules.example: Export: setup 1m, profit 0.5m a year, payback 2 years. Licence: setup 0.2m, profit 0.2m a year, payback 1 year, but little control. Local company: setup 6m, profit 1.8m a year, payback 6/1.8 = 3.3 years. With a high cultural score of 4 the licence is safer; with a 3-year time limit the local company fails the test.
modules.activity: Compare three entry options for the market you scored in module 2 and choose one with reasons.
modules.standard: Three paybacks are correct and the choice agrees with the stated time limit.

modules.title: Writing the exposure profile memo
modules.intro: The profile memo pulls the audit into one page a board can act on.
points: Lead with the answer
Show three numbers that matter
End with a recommended limit for each country
modules.example: Memo opening: 'We recommend capping country C at 15% of sales.' Evidence: C now 22% of sales (44m of 200m), expected political loss 5.2m, distance score 3.4. Working: 15% of 200m = 30m, so 14m of sales growth should go elsewhere. A board can say yes or no to this in one minute.
modules.activity: Write a one-page memo using your own results from modules 1 to 6, with one recommended limit.
modules.standard: One page, answer first, at least three correct numbers from earlier work, one limit with its working.

modules.title: Governance checks and the exposure wargame
modules.intro: Limits only work if someone checks them. We set the checks and then test them in a role-play where a shock hits.
points: Set a limit, an owner and a review date
Define a trigger that forces action
Run a shock and revise the plan
modules.example: Rule: no country over 25% of sales or 40% of any input. A shock cuts country C sales by 30%: 44m x 0.30 = 13.2m lost, which is 6.6% of total sales. The firm stays within its profit floor if costs fall 4m. The team checks whether the plan names who cuts which 4m.
modules.activity: In a group role-play, one team applies a shock and the others adjust limits and answer questions for 15 minutes.
modules.standard: The revised plan names an owner and date for each action and the loss figure is correct.

quiz.q: Four countries give a firm 60%, 20%, 12% and 8% of sales. What is the concentration score?
Why can a plain sum of distance scores mislead?
quiz.a: It treats all distance types as equally important, but a product may depend mostly on one, such as shipping for fresh goods.

quiz.q: Cultural 4, administrative 2, geographic 3, economic 5 with weights 20, 20, 40, 20. What is the weighted score?
Costs of 30m euro and sales of 10m euro. What is the net exposure and what does a 10% rise in the euro do?
quiz.a: Net short 20m euro; cost rises by 2m.

quiz.q: With a 60% hedge on a 20m exposure, how much is still open?
A risk has a 25% chance and an 8m impact. What is its expected loss?
Why does a 5% chance of a 40m loss need its own plan even though it is rare?
quiz.a: Its expected loss is 2.0m, the same as a common risk, and the actual hit would be very large.

quiz.q: Output is 130m and a 55% supplier fails for 6 weeks. What output is lost?
An option costs 6m and earns 1.8m a year. What is its payback?
Country C is 44m of 200m sales and the cap is 15%. How much sales must move elsewhere?
quiz.a: The cap is 30m, so 14m must move.

ladder.title: L1 Basic: What exposure means
ladder.slide: Exposure is the share of the firm that depends on one country. It covers sales, costs, assets and staff.
ladder.notes: Say: think of the firm as a table with four legs. Check: ask who can name one leg. Mistake: counting only sales.

ladder.title: L2 Concentration in numbers
ladder.slide: Shares squared and added give a score from 0 to 1. Higher means more reliance on few countries.
ladder.notes: Say: do the sum slowly on the board. Check: learners compute a four-country case. Mistake: forgetting to square.

ladder.title: L3 Four kinds of distance
ladder.slide: Cultural, administrative, geographic and economic distance each get a 1 to 5 score.
ladder.notes: Say: give one example of each type. Check: score a familiar market. Mistake: scoring on opinion without a reason.

ladder.title: L4 Weighting by product
ladder.slide: The same market is near for one product and far for another. Weights show which distance matters.
ladder.notes: Say: compare software with fresh fish. Check: weights add to 100. Mistake: equal weights by default.

ladder.title: L5 Money and risk in the numbers
ladder.slide: Net currency exposure, expected loss and supplier loss turn worry into figures.
ladder.notes: Say: every risk needs a chance and an impact. Check: check one product by hand. Mistake: ignoring rare big risks.

ladder.title: L6 Choosing an entry route
ladder.slide: Payback, control and distance together decide between export, licence or local company.
ladder.notes: Say: no option wins on every measure. Check: ask what time limit applies. Mistake: choosing on profit alone.

ladder.title: L7 Setting limits and testing them
ladder.slide: A limit needs an owner, a trigger and a review. A shock exercise shows whether it works.
ladder.notes: Say: run the shock live. Check: is each action owned? Mistake: limits with no owner.

rubric.not_yet: Several shares, scores or losses are wrong.
rubric.meets: All main figures are correct and the working is shown.
rubric.exceeds: Figures are correct, cross-checked and tested with a second case.

rubric.not_yet: Distance is described but not scored.
rubric.meets: Four distance types are scored with reasons and sensible weights.
rubric.exceeds: Weights are justified for the product and the effect on the choice is shown.

rubric.meets: A clear limit or option with supporting numbers.
rubric.exceeds: A recommendation that also states what would change it.

rubric.not_yet: No owners or review points; unclear writing.
rubric.meets: Owners, dates and triggers are named; the memo is clear.
rubric.exceeds: The plan stands up to questions in the role-play and is brief and persuasive.

jobs.what: Decides which countries the firm should grow in and sets the limits.
Measures country, supplier and currency risks and reports them to the board.
Runs a group of markets and keeps them inside the agreed limits.
Compares entry routes and prepares cases for new markets.
